1:
The opening notice — that the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard the returned exiles were building — sends the witnesses first to fix who these adversaries were, and then to the long enmity the verse quietly reopens. On the identity they are of one mind. The reformed John Gill names them the Samaritans; the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley calls them the relics of the ten tribes and the foreigners who had joined with them; and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott describes a mixed race whose original Israelite element had been all but lost among the heathen tribes planted in the north by Sargon, Sennacherib, and Esar-haddon, as recorded in 2 Kings 17:24-34. Adam Clarke, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, adds only that these were the several nations with which the kings of Assyria had peopled the land after carrying its first inhabitants into captivity.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the verse into a theology of opposition. Here, he says, is an instance of the old enmity put between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent: God's temple cannot be built but Satan will rage, and the gates of hell will fight against it. Yet in this very struggle Henry finds the second house exalted above the first, for Solomon built when there was neither adversary nor evil occurrent, as 1 Kings 5:4 attests, whereas this temple rose in the teeth of great opposition, so that in the overcoming of it the wisdom, power, and goodness of God were the more glorified and the church encouraged to trust him. The gospel kingdom, he notes, would in like manner be set up with much contention.

Henry dwells too on the names the chapter uses. The builders are called the children of the captivity, a title that makes them look very little: newly come out of bondage, born in it, still bearing its marks, and under the control of those whose captives they had lately been — yet the memory of that captivity, incurred by their neglect of the temple, is what quickens them now to the work. The opposers, by contrast, are the adversaries not of the Chaldeans or Persians, who let them build and welcome, but the patched-together people who feared the LORD and served their own gods too, the mongrel religion described in 2 Kings 17:33. The worst enemies Judah and Benjamin had, Henry warns, were these who said they were Jews and were not, an anticipation of the synagogue of Satan in Revelation 3:9. The witnesses converge: a restored remnant, scarcely settled, meets at once the fixed hostility of a half-pagan neighbour who will shortly clothe its malice in the language of friendship.
2:
The overture itself — "Let us build with you; for we seek your God, as ye do; and we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esar-haddon" — the witnesses read as a study in plausible treachery. The reformed John Gill marks the shrewdness of the approach: the Samaritans came to Zerubbabel and the chief of the fathers, the principal men, knowing that if these could not be won over the whole design must fail. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley strips the courtesy bare — this they spake not sincerely, but that by joining themselves to the work they might pry into the Jews' counsels and so find some matter of accusation against them. Adam Clarke agrees that for all their profession to acknowledge the same God and to be solicitous for his glory, the context proves they came with no friendly intention.

On the claim "we seek your God, as ye do" the witnesses turn to the record of the Samaritans' actual religion. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott recalls the verdict of 2 Kings 17:33 — "they feared the LORD, and served their own gods" — so that the applicants came either in the spirit of hypocrites or with a mind to blend their own idolatries with the pure worship of Jehovah; either way they are to be counted enemies of the God of Israel. Wesley reads the clause the same way: they did indeed seek him, but in a mongrel fashion, the syncretism described in 2 Kings 17:26 and following.

The appeal to Esar-haddon draws the chronologers. Ellicott observes that this king ended his reign about 668 B.C., so that the Samaritans speak from a tradition reaching back a century and a half; and in saying he "brought us up hither" they conveniently leave out of account whatever remnant of true Israel was still to be found among them. Wesley identifies Esar-haddon as the son of Sennacherib and his successor on the throne of Assyria, and canvasses whether the colonists were planted in the days of Shalmaneser — Esar-haddon serving then as one of his commanders — or whether Esar-haddon sent a second colony of his own to strengthen the first. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the smooth words masked a double purpose: to infiltrate the work and to lay the ground of a charge, so that the very offer to build was itself the opening move toward preventing the building altogether. What looked like an outstretched hand of fellowship was, on every reading, a probe sent out by men who worshipped after their own sort and meant the returned remnant no good.
3:
The refusal is blunt — "Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God; but we ourselves together will build" — and the witnesses defend it as principled rather than proud. The reformed John Gill notes that the answer came from the prince Zerubbabel, the high priest Joshua, and the chief of the people together, the whole leadership speaking with one voice. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the Hebrew: the reply means "it is not for you and for us to build a house to our God" — you and we cannot jointly raise a temple to the God who is ours — and by the deliberate stress on "our God" and "Jahve the God of Israel" the leaders quietly give the lie to the visitors' claim, "we seek your God as ye do." The phrase rendered "we ourselves together" carries the sense we alone, without your assistance.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the ground of the refusal as difference of covenant and nation. Adam Clarke has the leaders say, in effect, that they cannot acknowledge the Samaritans as worshippers of the true God, nor participate with them in anything pertaining to his worship. John Wesley makes the same point — the applicants were of another nation and religion, and so had no share in the grant of Cyrus, which was confined to the Israelites — and draws the practical lesson: take heed whom you go partners with, and on whose hand you lean; while we trust God with an absolute confidence, we must trust men with a prudent caution.

The fullest defence comes from the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, who anticipates the charge of bigotry and answers it from history. A careful study of 2 Kings 17, he argues, shows that the stern refusal of the leaders was precisely in harmony with the will of God; there was in it nothing of the intolerant spirit sometimes imagined, for the whole design of the Great Restoration would have been defeated by a single concession at this point. To admit the half-pagan Samaritans as co-builders would have been to poison the restored worship at its source. Ellicott adds that the appeal to Cyrus's command was a second and really subordinate justification, pleaded by men who were, after all, subjects of the Persian king whose decree was absolute and exclusive. The witnesses stand together: the door shut here was shut not from narrowness but from fidelity, and the purity of the second temple's worship hung upon the leaders' refusal to buy help at the price of compromise.
4:
When the friendly overture failed, the opposition changed its face — "then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building" — and the witnesses trace both the tactics and the words. The reformed John Gill lists the means the adversaries used: threatening the builders, dissuading the workmen from going on, labouring to cut off the supply of materials from the Tyrians and Zidonians bargained with in Ezra 3:7, and blocking the money out of the king's revenues that had been ordered for the expense. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sums it in a phrase: they discouraged and opposed the work by every possible means.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch settle the terms and the grammar. "The people of the land" are the colonists dwelling in the country, the very same whom verse 1 had called the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin; and the construction — the verb of being followed by a participle — expresses not a single act but the continuance of these hostile attempts, a steady, wearing pressure rather than one blow. To "weaken the hands" of a man, they explain, is to rob him of the strength and courage he needs for action, the same idiom used of those who disheartened Jeremiah in Jeremiah 38:4. By "the people of Judah" is meant the whole body of returned exiles, Benjamites included, Judah now standing for the entire territory of the new community as it had once stood for the southern kingdom.

Keil and Delitzsch pause too over a nicety of the text: where the written form gives one word for "troubling" them, the margin offers a reading from a root meaning to terrify or alarm, the same used at 2 Chronicles 32:18, so that the harassment aimed at fear as much as at delay. The picture the witnesses build is of a campaign of attrition. Having been denied a share in the work, the people of the land set themselves to make the work impossible — starving it of hands, of materials, and of money, and unnerving the more timid of the builders until the zeal that had begun so bravely began to flag. It is the second stage of the serpent's craft: what open partnership could not corrupt, quiet sabotage would try to strangle, and the discouragement sown here prepares the way for the hired counsellors and the formal accusations that the following verses will bring to the Persian court.
5:
The adversaries now carry the fight from the building-site to the palace — "and hired counsellors against them, to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus... even until the reign of Darius" — and the witnesses examine both the method and the span of years. The reformed John Gill supposes the hired men were set either to persuade the Persian officers in the province not to release the promised money, or to work upon the great men at court to get the edict of Cyrus revoked. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch leave the exact means open — whether the bribing of royal ministers or the retaining of legal agents to plead against the Jewish community at court and obtain an inhibition — but note the effect: the machinations, begun as soon as the foundation was laid, succeeded in stopping the work "all the days of Koresh," the remaining five years of Cyrus's sole reign over Babylon, the interruption falling, on the reckoning drawn from Daniel 10:2, in the beginning of his third year.

The stretch "until the reign of Darius" opens a chronological question the witnesses answer with one voice. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke identifies the persons corrupted as some of the principal officers of the Persian court, through whom the orders of Cyrus were either not executed or so slowly executed as to be almost useless, and takes the Darius in view to be Darius the son of Hystaspes. Charles Ellicott fills in the intervening reigns: the paid agents were kept at court for some eight years, till about 529 B.C.; then Cambyses succeeded his father and died in 522; then followed the usurping pseudo-Smerdis, whose few months Darius refused to reckon, dating his own accession from 522 — so that a comparison of the dates fixes this as the first Darius, Hystaspes' son.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley knits the same span into the human story behind it. Cyrus himself continued to favour the Jews, but was now diverted by his wars, and had left his son Cambyses as viceroy — a wicked prince and an enemy to the Jews; and the phrase "until Darius," Wesley insists, is really "and until," covering not the reign of Cyrus only but those of Cambyses and of the magician who came after, down to Darius at last. The witnesses converge on a sobering point: the enemies of the work did not need force, only patience and gold. By keeping a standing interest of bribed counsellors at the heart of the empire, they turned the machinery of a friendly government against its own decree, and the temple lay unbuilt for the better part of a generation — not because the king had forbidden it, but because his servants had been bought.
6:
With this verse the narrative leaps forward out of its strict order, gathering into one place the later assaults on the work, and the witnesses must first settle whose reign is meant. "In the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, wrote they unto him an accusation." The reformed John Gill records that Jarchi took this Ahasuerus for the husband of Esther, but that most, with Josephus, understand Cambyses the son and successor of Cyrus — a prince at enmity with the Egyptians who, fearing the Jews might side with them, was no friend to the returned exiles; his enemies seized the death of Cyrus and the first opportunity of the new reign to strike. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott concur that Ahasuerus is another name for Cambyses, who reigned some seven years and throughout that time let the building languish, while John Wesley, also wesleyan-arminian, notes that Ahasuerus was a common royal name and that this Cambyses was known to be no friend to the Jewish nation.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make the identification of these kings the very hinge of the section, insisting that the right understanding of the whole passage turns on the question, what Persian monarchs are meant by Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes — an answer to be gathered partly from the contents of the letter that follows. The word rendered "accusation," they add, is one that occurs only here, derived from a root meaning to bear enmity; its very form betrays the letter's purpose, though the substance of this first complaint is not given, only its hostile character.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the intrigue in a larger light. Cyrus had steadfastly adhered to the Jews' interest and supported his own grant, and while he lived it was to no purpose to offer anything against them; but his successor, whom Henry too takes for Cambyses, had no such knowledge of the God of Israel and no regard for the despised Jews. See, Henry urges, how watchful the church's enemies are to take the first opportunity of doing it a mischief — let not its friends be less careful to do it a kindness. The letter, he observes, is called an accusation, and in it the old serpent is at his ancient work: the devil is the accuser of the brethren, as Revelation 12:10 declares, and here he acts through the mouths of his instruments, employing men to make the godly odious to the many and obnoxious to the mighty. The witnesses agree that the reign changed, the protector was gone, and the accusers, patient and ready, struck the moment the throne passed to a king who cared nothing for Jerusalem.
7:
The complaint now shifts to a second king — "in the days of Artaxerxes wrote Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest" — and here the witnesses openly divide over who this Artaxerxes was. The reformed John Gill holds him the same as the Ahasuerus just named, that is Cambyses, Artaxerxes being a common style of the Persian kings; he weighs and rejects the guess that it was Smerdis the magian impostor who reigned between Cambyses and Darius, reasoning that a usurper of but seven months would scarcely have been written to and an answer received, and that Smerdis in any case courted the nations he ruled, proclaiming to them freedom from tribute. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees with Gill: this is Cambyses still, called by his Chaldee name Ahasuerus in the previous verse and here by his Persian name Artaxerxes, the name by which he styled himself in the correspondence.

Against them stand two voices who identify a different man. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke argues that after the death of Cambyses one of the Magi — variously called Oropaestus, Smerdis, Mardus, and Sphendatates by the ancient writers — usurped the empire, feigning himself to be the murdered brother of Cambyses, and that this pretender is the Artaxerxes of the text; Xerxes and Artaxerxes, he adds, were titles assumed by the Persian sovereigns whatever their earlier names. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the same view with a grammatical hint: this must be Gomates, the Magian priest who personated Smerdis and reigned only seven months, and Ezra marks the difference by writing "in the days of" rather than "in the reign of" as in the verse before. Ellicott notes that many commentators have instead made this Artaxerxes the Longimanus of the later chapters, identifying the earlier Ahasuerus with Xerxes; but the strict sequence of events, and the word "ceased" that binds verse 23 to verse 24, tell against it — while granting that the Persian princes often bore more than one name and that such a parenthetical insertion is not impossible.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch stand back from the roll of names to make the point on which all the labour turns: the whole understanding of the section depends on which monarchs are meant, and the answer must be sought in the letter itself. On the writers there is no dispute. Rehum, styled "lord of counsel," was the royal counsellor or Persian civil governor, and Shimshai the scribe his secretary; and the letter, all agree, was drawn up and interpreted in the Syrian or Aramaic tongue — which is why, from this verse, Ezra's own record changes language. So the witnesses leave a genuine unsettled question — Cambyses or the false Smerdis — while agreeing that whoever sat on the throne, the machinery of accusation was now formally engaged.
8:
The verse names the two men who framed the accusation — "Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem" — and the witnesses attend to their offices and to a striking feature of the record itself. The reformed John Gill takes this to be the same letter already spoken of, and reports Jarchi's account that it was sent in the name of Mithredath and Tabeel and their company, its matter composed by Rehum as master of sense and set down in writing by Shimshai the scribe — whom the old rabbi fancifully made a son of Haman — though Gill judges it was written rather in the name of them all together. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the titles: Rehum "the chancellor" is the lord of judgment, the counsellor of the Persian king, a conventional style of the civil governor, and Shimshai "the scribe" is the royal secretary.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes on what happens to the text at this point, and turns a dry philological fact into an argument for the book's trustworthiness. With this verse, he observes, the Aramaic or Chaldee portion of Ezra begins, and it runs on unbroken to Ezra 6:18: the officials wrote to the king in their own language, and the king returned his answer in the same dialect. This circumstance, Clarke argues, adds authenticity to the whole; so scrupulous was the inspired penman that he gave not merely the substance of what each party spoke and wrote, but their very words, and those words in the very language and character in which they had been conceived. The historian, in other words, has copied his documents rather than paraphrased them.

The witnesses do not divide, and their small notes gather to a single observation. What is recorded here is not the sacred writer's own summary of the affair but the actual instrument of the accusation — a real letter, from named officers holding known offices, preserved in the tongue in which it was drafted. Ellicott's care over the titles and Clarke's over the language point the same way: the opposition to the temple was no vague popular grumbling but a formal, documented act of state, lodged by the machinery of Persian provincial government and entered, word for word, into the record — so that later readers might see with their own eyes by what arts good work is hindered and good people traduced. Gill's willingness to correct even Jarchi's guess about the writers shows the same concern for the plain fact of the case: whoever held the pen, the charge went up in the name of the whole hostile confederacy.
9:
The letter's long roll of subscribers — "the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites" — the witnesses read as the muster of a whole transplanted population arrayed against Jerusalem. The reformed John Gill takes them for the governors of the several nations, all of whom set their hands to the letter. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note the awkward turn of the sentence: after the naming of Rehum and Shimshai the reader looks for the letter to begin, but is given instead a full catalogue of the senders, an anacoluthon whose loose grammar leaves the main verb hanging until the copy is at last introduced. The whole list, they judge, stood in the superscription of the actual document, piled up on purpose to lend the complaint the weight of numbers.

Charles Ellicott, of the same grammatical-historical school, works through the names as far as they can be traced. The Apharsites and Dehavites are Persians; the Babylonians are the old races of Babylon, the men of Cuthah and Ava planted in the land according to 2 Kings 17:24; the Susanchites are colonists from Susa; the Apharsathchites are probably the Pharathiakites, a predatory people of Media; and the Archevites are inhabitants of Erech, the ancient city named in Genesis 10:10. The Dinaites and Tarpelites, he admits, can be identified only by conjecture.

Beneath the antiquarian detail the witnesses find a single point worth pressing. This is the very population whose mongrel origin the earlier verses had exposed — Assyria's patchwork of deported peoples, gathered from Babylon and Susa and Media and settled in the cities of Samaria — now closing ranks as one against the small returned remnant. The names that seem at first a mere formality of Persian bureaucracy are in fact the signature of the whole heathen north, and the number and variety of the subscribers is itself part of the intimidation: a solitary community of former captives is made to face what looks like the united voice of every nation round about. Keil and Delitzsch's observation that the list was heaped up "to give weight" catches the intent exactly; the accusers meant the king to feel the pressure of a crowd, and the very clumsiness of the sentence betrays how eager they were to parade every name they could enlist. The catalogue, dull as it reads, is the roll of a coalition of convenience against the worship of the God of Israel.
10:
The superscription closes by tracing the colonists to their planter — "the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Asnappar brought over, and set in the cities of Samaria" — and the witnesses puzzle over who this Asnappar was. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confesses the uncertainty plainly: whether Asnappar was Shalmaneser, or Esar-haddon, or some other, the learned and the chronologers are not agreed; the Syriac calls him Asphid, but of him no more is really known, and he may have been merely the military officer appointed to escort the colony into the land. John Wesley, of the same school, leans toward Esar-haddon or some other person of eminence, the captain who conducted the colony hither. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is more decided on the negative side: Asnappar cannot be Esar-haddon himself, but was probably his chief officer.

On the geography the witnesses agree. The reformed John Gill and Wesley alike take "whom he brought over" of the river Euphrates, the great boundary across which the deportees were carried westward into Samaria. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch add that the recurring formula "and at such a time," which the older versions found so baffling, means no more than "and so forth," a scribe's shorthand for the full titles and date that stood in the original.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the letter's opening claim, that the Jews "came up from thee to us," and guard against a false inference. The phrase means simply that the exiles had come from the territory where the king then held his court, that is from the country beyond the Euphrates; it does not imply, as some have supposed, that these particular Jews had been transported to Jerusalem by Artaxerxes himself. The witnesses thus leave the person of Asnappar a genuine and confessed obscurity — a great Assyrian name, or his officer, lost in the mist of a policy of mass deportation — while agreeing on the thing that matters for the argument: the accusers were themselves a people brought in from elsewhere, strangers settled on the land by an imperial hand, and their complaint against the true heirs of the soil came from mouths that had themselves been planted there by conquest. The very sentence in which they claim the king's protection betrays that they were colonists, not natives, of the country they now presumed to defend against the returning children of Judah.
11:
Before quoting the accusation, Ezra pauses to mark it as a transcript — "this is the copy of the letter that they sent unto him" — and the witnesses note both the document and a stubborn phrase within it. The reformed John Gill observes simply that this is the letter Ezra had brought with him from Babylon, its text contained in the five verses that follow, so that what we read is a genuine copy lodged among the Persian records and afterward drawn out by Ezra for his history — the enemies' own indictment turned, by the providence that governs even hostile archives, into a permanent witness against themselves.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the words "and at such a time," which he says have greatly perplexed all commentators and critics. The ancient versions give no clear light: the Vulgate renders it "and they wish prosperity," as though it were a salutation; others turn it "and so forth"; and the early English Bibles, uncertain, treated the Hebrew as the name of a people — Coverdale's "in Canaan," Becke's "in Ceneeth" with a marginal "or peace," Barker's "and Cheeneth" glossed as "a certain people that envied the Jews." All this, Clarke concludes, is mere guessing in the midst of obscurity; and he inclines to Calmet's emendation, which by a slight change reads "and at this time," a courteous wish that the king might enjoy at all future seasons the health and prosperity he then possessed — a sense, he adds, not remote from the Chaldee original.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott cuts through the tangle with a plainer verdict. The address "on this side the river" means, from the writers' standpoint, beyond the river Euphrates, the phrase framed as it would sound at the Persian court; and "and at such a time" is best rendered "and so forth," a shorthand pointing back to the full style already set out — "thy servants, as aforesaid." The witnesses do not finally divide over the sense: whether one follows Calmet's "at this time" or Ellicott's "and so forth," the clause is a formula of courtly address, not a hidden clue. What Gill's note keeps before us is the larger fact — that the sacred historian has preserved the enemies' own words with their salutation and all, so that the reader may weigh the accusation exactly as it was laid, and see for himself the craft with which the letter opens in the smooth language of loyal servants before it proceeds to its slanders. The very fidelity of the transcript, the witnesses imply, is part of Scripture's honesty: it does not paraphrase the enemy into a caricature, but sets down his flattery word for word, so that the reader may judge the whole for himself.
12:
The letter comes to its charge — "the Jews which came up from thee to us are come unto Jerusalem, building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up the walls thereof, and joined the foundations" — and the witnesses expose it as a compound of malice and untruth. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds virulence, craft, and exaggeration stamped on every sentence; yet he notes that even here the accusers say only that the Jews are preparing the walls and joining the foundations, a charge they will presently sharpen in verse 13 and verse 16.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses hardest on the falsehood of the thing. Very careful, he says, were the accusers to inform the king that the Jews had set up the walls of the city — nay, in the margin, had finished them — and joined the foundations, when this was utterly far from the case. The returned exiles had only begun to build the temple, which Cyrus had commanded them to build; as for the walls, nothing was done or so much as designed toward their repair, as appears from the ruinous state in which Nehemiah found them long after in Nehemiah 1:3. What shall be done, Henry asks with the psalmist, to these false tongues, nay these false pens — sharp arrows of the mighty and coals of juniper, as Psalms 120:3-4 has it? Had the writers not been lost to all honour, and very sure of the king's favour, they durst not have written to him what all their neighbours knew to be a notorious lie.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same in a sentence: the whole is a mere fiction, which, being confidently affirmed, they thought would easily find belief with a king whose heart and ears they already possessed through their hired counsellors. The reformed John Gill notes only that this was the point the letter existed to lodge — that it might be known to the king that Jerusalem was rising again — while the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch remark, on the words "which came up from thee," that they mean no more than that the Jews had come from the country beyond the Euphrates where the king held court, not that he had sent them. The witnesses stand together: the accusation trades a modest truth — that a temple was being built — for a dangerous falsehood — that a fortress-city was being walled — and calculates that a distant king, fed by bribed informers, will not trouble to tell the difference. The name of the loyal city of David is turned, by a stroke of the pen, into "the rebellious and the bad city."
13:
The accusers now supply a motive of state — "if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings" — and the witnesses parse both the taxes and the threat. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch identify the three imposts as distinct kinds of levy: a measured tax or tribute, a duty on consumption, and a toll paid upon the roads by travellers and their goods — the same triad that recurs in verse 20 and Ezra 7:24. The rare word closing the sentence they take to mean "at last" or "in the future," so that the clause warns the city will "at length bring damage to the king." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke offers his own division — a capitation tax, an excise on merchandise, and a sort of land tax — and paraphrases the sting: permit these people to fortify their city, and they will soon set you at naught and pay you no kind of tribute at all. Charles Ellicott renders the members a little differently again — toll for the highways, custom as a provision in kind, tribute as the money tax — and corrects the last phrase to read that "at length damage will be done to the kings."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry exposes the argument as groundless prognostication. The writers were confident, and would have the king believe on their bare word, that a rebuilt Jerusalem would refuse all tribute, and — since a great lie is as soon spoken as a little one — that the whole country beyond the river would follow her into revolt, so that the crown would lose its revenue and a conniving prince would wrong not himself only but his successors. Every line of it, Henry says, breathes the subtlety and the malice of the old serpent.

The reformed John Gill adds only that the matter was pressed on the king to be seriously and thoroughly weighed by himself and his counsellors. The witnesses converge on the cleverness of the appeal: the accusers had found the one argument certain to move a Persian king — the fear of lost taxes and a rebellious frontier. They could not prove the Jews disloyal, so they predicted disloyalty; they could not show a fortress, so they conjured the revenue it would one day cost. It is the ancient slander, Henry observes elsewhere, that the prosperity of the church is hurtful to kings and princes, though nothing could be more false, since true godliness teaches men to honour and obey their sovereign. The lie is aimed straight at the treasury, because that is where a distant emperor is most easily alarmed.
14:
The accusers now clothe their malice in the dress of loyalty — "because we have maintenance from the king's palace, and it was not meet for us to see the king's dishonour, therefore have we sent and certified the king" — and the witnesses linger over the vivid figure of the salt. The reformed John Gill notes that the word rendered "maintenance" is literally "salt": these men held posts under the king to which salaries were annexed, and since offices of honour and trust were anciently paid in salt, such rewards came, as Pliny observed, to be called salaria. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm that "to salt salt" is to eat salt, and that to eat the salt of the palace is a figure for being in the king's pay; they note in passing the older rabbinic fancy, which Luther followed, that read the clause as "we who have destroyed the temple," from the custom of strewing salt on a ruined place in Judges 9:45 — a reading they set aside.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enriches the image with its moral weight. To be salted at all times with the salt of the palace is to live on the king's bounty and to owe him fidelity; salt was the emblem of an incorruptible covenant, and those who ate bread and salt together were held to have entered a solemn bond. So the accusers intimate that their very consciences are pledged to the king's interest — hypocrites, Clarke judges, who were probably in the Persian pay and made a show of the obligation. Charles Ellicott agrees that the phrase is a general expression for dependence on the king, whose loss or dishonour they profess themselves unwilling to behold.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the pretence into a mirror. See, he says, how a secret enmity to Christ and his gospel is often gilded over with a pretended affection to Caesar and his power — the very men who hated Rome could yet cry, to serve a turn, "we have no king but Caesar." But Henry will not leave the salt to the hypocrites. If those who lived upon the crown thought themselves bound in gratitude to guard its honour, how much more reason have we, who have our whole maintenance from the God of heaven and are salted with his salt, living upon his bounty and kept by his providence, to resent his dishonour and do what we can to prevent it. The witnesses agree that the plea is a mask: a claim of tender loyalty pressed by men whose real interest was to keep the Jews weak, and whose fine talk of the king's honour was, as the letter's own falsehoods prove, worth exactly nothing.
15:
To their prediction the accusers add an appeal to the archives — "that search may be made in the book of the records of thy fathers... and know that this city is a rebellious city, and hurtful unto kings and provinces, and that they have moved sedition within the same of old time" — and the witnesses examine both the record invoked and the exaggeration that colours the appeal. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that the "book of the records" is the public royal chronicle in which the chief events of the realm were entered, the same volume that in Esther 6:1 is called the book of the records of the daily events. "Thy fathers," they add, are the king's predecessors in government, not his ancestors only — so the term reaches back through the Median and Persian to the Chaldean and Assyrian kings whose dominion the Persians had inherited.

The reformed John Gill reads the phrase the same way, taking it of the records of the Babylonian monarchy and, since the Medes and Persians were joined with it, of theirs also. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke likewise refers it to the records of the Chaldeans, to whom the Persians succeeded. Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, agrees that the register extended beyond the king's own fathers back to the predecessors of the Median dynasty, and fastens on the tell-tale colouring of the language: the phrase "of old time" is really "from the days of eternity," time out of mind, and "the spirit of exaggeration, if not of falsehood, appears in every word here."

That is the point on which the witnesses gather. The appeal to the archives is shrewd, for it invites the king to verify the charge and so lends it an air of candour; and there was, as later verses concede, some colour to it — Jerusalem had indeed thrown off the yoke of Babylon in her last kings. But the accusers inflate a partial truth into a timeless and total one, branding as an immemorial rebel a city whose recent captives had been bidden to seek the peace of the land of their exile. By sending the king to his own chronicles they mean to make the record itself their witness, trusting that an old and isolated fact of revolt, stated broadly enough, will be taken for the settled character of the place. It is slander armed with a footnote — the more dangerous because it points to something real, and counts on the king reading no further than the word "rebellious."
16:
The letter reaches its crescendo of alarm — "we certify the king that, if this city be builded again, and the walls thereof set up, by this means thou shalt have no portion on this side the river" — and the witnesses mark how far the exaggeration has now been carried. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the sentence as the climax of the whole indictment: having painted the Jews as habitual rebels, the accusers now warn that a rebuilt and fortified Jerusalem will cost the king his very supremacy west of the Euphrates — he will have no portion there, nothing more to do with the provinces beyond the river, his sway over the whole region forfeited.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, calls it the same unscrupulous use of language, and measures it against the facts. If the river meant is the Euphrates, the threat is wildly disproportionate: only in the days of Solomon, and once or twice after, had Israel's rule reached toward that river, and it was in the last degree unlikely they should ever do so again. The letter, Ellicott allows, may have been meant more loosely — to hint that Jerusalem might become a centre of general disaffection among the western provinces — but as it stands it charges a handful of returned exiles, scarcely able to raise a temple, with the power to tear a satrapy from the Persian crown.

The reformed John Gill notes simply that the accusers spoke of the city as being rebuilt "as it formerly was," and as now, on their telling, attempted. The witnesses agree on the shape of the thing: the complaint has climbed by steps from a modest falsehood to an enormous one. First the walls were said to be rising; then the tribute was said to be threatened; now the empire itself is said to be at stake. Each stage magnifies the last, until a small and defenceless community stands accused of endangering the king's dominion over all the lands from Judah to the great river. It is the method of every such accusation — to make the feeblest object of its malice appear a mortal danger to the state — and the witnesses let the sheer extravagance of the charge condemn it, since the very men who could not keep a supply of timber flowing to their building-site are here represented as able to strip a Persian king of half his realm. The false letter ends, fittingly, in the largest of its lies.
17:
The king's reply opens with a word of greeting — "then sent the king an answer... Peace, and at such a time" — and the witnesses first mark that he answered at all, and then how he answered. The reformed John Gill reads the very fact as a triumph for the adversaries: the affair, on examination, being found of importance, the king thought fit to send them a formal answer, which was to do them honour and to put into their hands the power and authority they had been angling for. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gloss the opening term as a decree or sentence — a word, they note, drawn from the Persian and passed into Hebrew — and take the salutation "peace, and so forth" as the courtly formula of a royal letter; Charles Ellicott agrees that it is a "salutation, and so forth," observing that here, as in the accusers' own letter, the historian has blended the address and the opening of the reply. Adam Clarke notes only that the puzzling phrase is the same that met us in verse 10.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the reply as a lesson in the danger of one-sided information. The king of Persia, he says, suffered himself to be imposed upon by the fraud and falsehood of the Samaritans; he took no care to examine the allegations of their petition concerning what the Jews were actually doing, but took the charge for granted and showed himself very willing to gratify the accusers with an order to stay the work. See here, Henry urges, the hard fate of princes, who must see and hear with other men's eyes and ears, and give judgment upon things as they are represented to them, though often represented falsely.

Against that, Henry sets the one unfailing judge. God's judgment, he says, is always just, because he sees things as they are, and it is according to truth; where earthly kings are deceived by lying reports, the King of heaven cannot be. The witnesses converge on the sombre irony of the moment. A great empire's machinery has been set in motion by a letter that its own recipients never troubled to test; the accusers have won not merely a hearing but a royal warrant; and the very courtesy of the king's "peace" is about to become the instrument of a violent stoppage. Gill's note that the answer honoured the adversaries and Henry's that it was won by fraud meet in a single point: the reply is gracious in form and disastrous in effect, a decree extracted from a deceived prince who judged a cause he had never examined.
18:
The royal answer proper begins — "the letter which ye sent unto us hath been plainly read before me" — and the witnesses, though few here, draw out the two features of the sentence. The reformed John Gill observes the courtly plural "unto us," which had by now become the settled style of kings speaking of themselves, a small mark of the majesty in which the reply is couched. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the disputed word rendered "plainly." The participle, they insist, corresponds to the Hebrew for "made plain," used here adverbially — the letter was distinctly, articulately read aloud before the king — and does not mean, as some have taken it, "translated into Persian." What the verse records is a public, careful reading of the document in open court, not its rendering into another tongue.

That distinction carries more weight than it first appears. The accusers had begged the king to search and to know; the king answers that their letter has been read out before him with full attention, and that he has acted upon it — the machinery of the empire responding, point by point, to the charge as laid. Keil and Delitzsch link the clause forward to what follows: the king says he then gave commandment, and search was made, and it was found that this city had of old lifted itself up against kings — so that the "plain reading" of the letter is the first step in a process that runs on into the inquiry of the next verse.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very thinness of comment leaves the irony exposed. A letter thick with exaggeration and falsehood — walls that were not built, a revolt that was ancient and isolated, a threat to the empire that was pure invention — is here "plainly read" before the throne and taken at its word. The clarity is all in the reading, none in the truth; the document is heard distinctly and believed uncritically. The king's grave assurance that the letter has been carefully perused, so far from protecting the Jews, only lends the accusation the dignity of due process, and prepares the reader for the ruinous "and it is found" that the following verse will pronounce. What is read plainly, the witnesses quietly remind us, is not therefore read rightly, and the whole tragedy of the section turns on that gap between a clear hearing and a just one.
19:
The king reports the result of his inquiry — "I commanded, and search hath been made, and it is found that this city of old time hath made insurrection against kings, and that rebellion and sedition have been made therein" — and the witnesses weigh both the finding and the loaded word in which it is couched. The reformed John Gill takes the search to have been made in the records of the king's predecessors, whether Chaldean or Persian. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the key verb "lifted itself up" rebelliously, the same term used of Adonijah's self-exalting revolt in 1 Kings 1:5, and grant that the charge had a basis, since Jerusalem had in fact risen against the kings of Babylon in her last days.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes the moment for a sharp reflection on the politics of the word "insurrection." How true, he exclaims, is the proverb that it is an easy thing to find a staff to beat a dog. The struggles of the Israelites to preserve or regain the independence they held from God are here branded insurrection, rebellion, and sedition — and branded so only because they failed; had those struggles succeeded, such offensive names would never have been used. He draws the parallel of his own nation's history: in 1688 the people of England struggled to throw off an oppressive government that was overthrowing their religion and liberties, and because they prevailed it is called the Revolution; had they failed, it would have been called rebellion, and its leaders put to death. The victor writes the vocabulary.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a needed precision: whatever insurrection lay in Jerusalem's past, it was never against Persia, but only such revolts against Babylon as are alluded to in 2 Kings 24. The distinction matters, for the accusers had insinuated a settled disloyalty that would turn against the present crown, when the historical rebellions had all been against a fallen empire the Persians themselves had supplanted. The witnesses gather to a common irony. The king's "it is found" sounds like the sober verdict of research, and there was indeed something in the archives; but the something was old, was directed against another power, and had nothing to do with the small worshipping community now at work on a temple. A true fact, wrenched from its context and dressed in a hostile name, has been made to do the work of a lie — and Clarke's mordant proverb hangs over the whole: to a ruler resolved to strike, any record will furnish a stick.
20:
The king's memorandum continues — "there have been mighty kings also over Jerusalem, which have ruled over all countries beyond the river; and toll, tribute, and custom, was paid unto them" — and the witnesses agree at once on whom the words describe. The reformed John Gill names David and Solomon, whose empire the records would preserve. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch concur that the boast of a dominion over the whole region west of the Euphrates applies in its full extent only to David and Solomon, and in a fainter degree to some of the later kings of Israel and Judah. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, extends the line a little — David and Solomon, and a few kings down to Josiah, had extended their sway and made neighbouring nations tributary — and supposes the earlier kings' names would be cited historically, though they had no direct place in the Persian annals.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the proof-texts for the ancient greatness. "Beyond the river" means beyond the Euphrates, and both David and Solomon carried their conquests across it: David's victories are told in 2 Samuel 8:3, and of Solomon it is written in 1 Kings 4:21 that he reigned over all the kingdoms from the river to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt, the tributary empire the accusers now hold up as a warning.

Here the witnesses catch the real craft of the passage. The historical note is accurate — Jerusalem had indeed once ruled to the Euphrates and gathered tribute from the nations — but the accusers, and the king who echoes them, turn that faded glory into a present menace. The very greatness of David and Solomon is made an argument against the grandchildren of the exile, as though a people who could scarcely rebuild a ruined temple were on the verge of reconstituting an empire and diverting its taxes from Persia to themselves. Keil and Delitzsch's careful qualification — that the boast holds in its full extent only of David and Solomon — quietly deflates the threat: what was true of two great kings half a millennium before is no measure of what a struggling remnant might do now. The past is real, but it is being used as a scarecrow; and the king, persuaded that history must repeat itself, prepares to forbid the work on the strength of a splendour four centuries dead.
21:
The decree itself follows — "give ye now commandment to cause these men to cease, and that this city be not builded, until another commandment shall be given from me" — and the witnesses attend to the careful wording of the prohibition. The reformed John Gill notes plainly that the men are to be made to cease from building, the officers being given a direct charge to enforce the royal will. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the order "to hinder these people, that this city be not built until command be given from me," understanding the closing clause of a command to build — the work is stayed only until the king himself should license its resumption, so that even the prohibition carries within it the seed of its own reversal.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on that reservation as the one merciful thread in the sentence. The rebuilding, he observes, was only provisionally suspended: the decree amounts to "let it cease for the present, and let it not proceed at any time without an express order from me." The door was shut, but not bolted; the king kept the matter in his own hand, and left room for a later reversal that the providence of God would in time supply.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks a silence in the order that will prove momentous. Neither the accusers in their letter nor the king in his reply make any mention of the temple, or of the building of that; and Henry sees why. Both parties knew that the Jews had not merely a permission but a positive command from Cyrus to rebuild the house of God, which even these bold Samaritans had not the confidence to move him to repeal. They spoke only of the city — "let not that be built," that is, as a walled and gated fortress — and confined the royal prohibition to the walls. The witnesses thus expose a fault-line that the next verses will tear open. The decree, read strictly, forbade only the fortifying of Jerusalem, and left the temple untouched; it was provisional, awaiting the king's further word; and it kept the whole question open. Every safeguard in the wording — the limitation to the city, the "until another commandment," the reserved royal discretion — was a real restraint upon the adversaries. Whether they would honour those limits, or seize the order as a warrant for more than it said, is the question Henry leaves hanging over verse 23.
22:
The king closes his order with an anxious urgency — "take heed now that ye fail not to do this: why should damage grow to the hurt of the kings?" — and the witnesses catch both the pressure of the command and the motive behind it. The reformed John Gill reads it as a charge to put the orders into execution at once, without loss of time, obliging the Jews to desist from rebuilding the walls of their city — though, Gill is careful to add, the report of their doing so was a great falsehood. The king presses for speed against a danger that did not exist, and the very vehemence of his "fail not" measures how completely he had been deceived.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the warning more exactly: "be warned from committing an oversight in this matter" — take heed to overlook nothing, for the word carries the sense of one instructed and put on his guard. And the king's reason is naked self-interest: "why should the damage become great, so as to bring injury to kings?" It is the same fear of lost revenue that the accusers had planted in verse 13, now echoed back from the throne as the ground of the whole prohibition.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the note in a phrase: the king would not that the crown should lose anything by his wearing it. His concern is not for justice, nor for the truth of the charge he never examined, but for the imagined threat to his treasury; and so a distant emperor, moved by the fear of a tax he was never in danger of losing, lends the force of his empire to a lie. The witnesses let the smallness of the motive stand against the greatness of the harm. A word about revenue, pressed by bribed informers, is enough to arrest the rebuilding of the house of God; the king who could not be troubled to test the accusation is all diligence when his own profit seems at stake, urging his officers to "fail not" and to "take heed" in a cause that had no foundation but their malice. The verse thus closes the royal letter on the same low string it had been playing throughout — the security of the crown's income — and shows how easily the machinery of a great state is turned, by a fearful and ill-informed prince, to the service of the church's enemies.
23:
The decree is no sooner in hand than it is abused — "when the copy of king Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum, and Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went up in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power" — and the witnesses fasten on that haste and that force. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch translate the last words "hindered them by violence and force," defending the rendering of the rare term as arm or violence against Bertheau's milder "with forces and a host": what the adversaries brought was not an army so much as raw compulsion. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that they commanded the Jews on pain of the king's displeasure to proceed no further, obliging all to lay down their tools, and probably backing the order with an armed band.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley together expose the sleight by which the order was stretched. Their feet ran to evil, Henry says, borrowing the words of Proverbs 1:16; and as the accusers had abused the king in the obtaining of the order by their misinformations, so now they abused him in the executing of it. The royal decree, both witnesses insist, was only to prevent the walling of the city; but the adversaries, having force in their hands, construed it as reaching to the temple — for it was the temple against which their real enmity was set, and which they had all along wanted some colour to hinder. There was, Henry allows, a general clause bidding them "cause these men to cease," which properly referred to the walls; this they wilfully applied to the house of God.

The reformed John Gill notes only that the letter was read before those to whom it was particularly directed, setting the swift reaction in motion. From the abuse Wesley draws the standing lesson: see what need we have to pray, not for kings only, but for all in authority under them, since the quietness of our lives depends much on the integrity and wisdom of inferior magistrates as well as of the supreme. The witnesses converge on the tragedy of the moment. A limited, provisional order, wrung from a deceived king and touching only the city walls, becomes in the hands of eager enemies a warrant to stop the temple itself by violence. The safeguards written into the decree are trampled the instant it is read; malice supplies what the letter withheld; and the work of the house of God is halted not by the law as given but by the law as seized and twisted by men who ran to Jerusalem to do it.
24:
The long parenthesis closes and the narrative returns to its thread — "then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem. So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia" — and the witnesses gather to date the stoppage and to untangle the chapter's order. The reformed John Gill remarks that we are not told how far the work had gone — perhaps a little above the foundation — before it was discontinued. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the literary architecture: with this verse the narrator resumes the notice of verse 5, that the adversaries had succeeded in delaying the temple until the reign of Darius, and now adds the precise term — the second year of that king; the intervening section had turned aside to record the later accusations made to Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes. They warn that reading verses 23 and 24 as strictly successive gives the false impression that the cessation was the effect of the prohibition just obtained, whereas the stoppage belongs to the earlier reign.

On the identity of Darius and the span of years the witnesses are of one mind. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley names him Darius the son of Hystaspes, the successor of Cambyses, and Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical, judges it clear from the thread of the sacred history that it was this Darius. Adam Clarke fixes the chronology: the returned exiles began the work in the first year of Cyrus, about 536 B.C.; they were forced to desist about 522; and so it continued until the second year of Darius, about 519.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, agreeing that the record here returns to verse 5 with a more exact note of time, sets the whole affliction in a truer proportion. The suspension of the great enterprise — "the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem" — lasted, in its final phase, nearly two years; yet it must be remembered, he adds, that the altar remained all this while the centre of a certain worship, so that the interruption stopped the building but not the service of God. The witnesses leave the chapter on a note of suspended hope. The temple stands unfinished, its enemies triumphant for a season, the work silenced by fraud and force; but the silence is dated — "unto the second year of Darius" — and the very verse that records the stoppage already names the reign in which, as the next chapter will tell, the word of the LORD by Haggai and Zechariah would set the builders to their task again.
